In computational cardiac mechanics, solving the heart muscle's motion is often reduced to solving a large system of linear equations. Due to the large size of these equations, direct methods are impractical, so we rely on efficient iterative solvers. Multilevel preconditioners can significantly enhance convergence rates, but choosing the optimal type and structure of such preconditioners is challenging. This study compares the performance of eight scalable multilevel preconditioners combined with the GMRES iterative solver on a range of cardiac mechanics models. We evaluate their effectiveness in terms of convergence rates, memory and communication requirements, and computational speed. Our analysis shows that these preconditioners perform well across different types of models, but their performance varies greatly. Some preconditioners excel in certain scenarios but fall short in others, while others demonstrate consistent performance across the board. Our findings suggest that the INV-LLS and ELLANEOUS preconditioners are particularly effective in cardiac mechanics. These preconditioners' efficiency is largely unaffected by the level of subdomain division and domain connectivity. They also excel in models with irregular geometry and varying material properties. Our code is publicly available for download at https://github.com/CMCS-Group/LLS preconditioner. This repository includes the necessary code to replicate our results, as well as documentation for setting up and running the cardiac mechanics simulations. Our software is compatible with the PETSc library, a widely-used package for solving linear equations and other computational tasks. In the realm of Information Science, collaborative systems have garnered significant interest due to their potential for high productivity and efficient information sharing. Social tagging systems, characterized by user-generated labels and collaborative filtering mechanisms, have become prominent examples of successful collaboration in both scientific and real-world settings. These systems have demonstrated the ability to support large-scale information management and provide insights into the dynamics of human cognition. This paper aims to contribute to the existing knowledge on collaborative filtering by investigating previously unexplored aspects of social tagging systems, including (1) the extent of content reuse, (2) temporal dynamics in tagging processes, (3) interest alignment among system users, and (4) potential system collaborations. Our analysis of two large datasets from Del.icio.us and BibSon reveals that content reuse is prevalent, and temporal analysis of the systems shows that tagging processes follow a power-law distribution with significant variability. Furthermore, our results indicate that system users exhibit both individual and collective interest alignment, and we propose a method to identify groups of users with similar interests. Finally, our study demonstrates that system tags can be effectively utilized for collaborative system recommendations. This research provides a comprehensive understanding of the underlying mechanisms of social tagging systems, and its findings can guide the development of more effective collaborative systems. In complex environments, effective object recognition relies on identifying key characteristics beyond basic visual properties. This study demonstrates that sophisticated recurrent neural networks, designed for object categorization, leverage category-specific and interdependent object features to differentiate between objects. Through systematic modifications to a neural network architecture, we show that removing redundant features enhances its ability to distinguish between objects, highlighting the importance of unique information for accurate categorization. Furthermore, we observe that removing features specific to each object category causes the network to over-rely on low-level features, leading to decreased performance in object categorization. These findings are consistent across multiple datasets and network configurations, and we illustrate the significance of feature interactions through case studies in a dataset of 3D novel objects. Ultimately, this research underscores the significance of feature orthogonality in recurrent neural networks for object categorization.

To create a natural language conversation, a system must produce a response
that aligns with the user's intended role. This requires not only grasping the
context but also adhering to the user's language, which can be challenging
given the vast possibilities of human speech. To overcome this, we propose a
new framework that generates role-consistent text using large-scale language
models. Our approach involves representing a role by collecting and averaging
sentences that embody a role, then using this representation as a target in
the language model's minimization process. This targets a sentence that is
most likely to be perceived as coming from a particular role. Our results show
that this method produces responses that are 30-40% more likely to be
associated with a role, and when combined with a state-of-the-art language
model, our system outperforms a state-of-the-art open-domain dialogue model
by 10-20%. Our code and data are available for public use.

STRAND is trained in two stages: the first involves optimizing the ranking model, followed by adjusting the session embedding to align with the learned ranking structure. Experimental results demonstrate that STRAND outperforms existing session-based recommendation methods. significant improvements over PCL and robustness in keypoint noise scenarios. The

Moreover, our framework was successfully applied to multi-person scenarios, yielding results that were on par with state-of-the-art techniques. Deep learning-based medical image segmentation has shown significant advancements in recent years, primarily driven by the availability of annotated data. Nonetheless, obtaining precise segmentations in multiple imaging modalities is often hindered by the time-consuming process of acquiring and annotating images. This paper introduces an innovative approach, the cyclic division generative adversarial network (CDGAN), designed to perform multi-modal image segmentation without requiring labeled data. The proposed method integrates two neural networks, a forward model and a division model, which work in tandem to generate accurate segmentations in both modalities. The forward model generates a segmentation boundary in one modality, which is then utilized by the division model to obtain the corresponding segmentation in the other modality through a transformation operation. The training process is facilitated by adversarial loss functions that promote realistic segmentation outputs and accurate two-way segmentation mappings. Experimental results on two datasets demonstrate the efficacy of the CDGAN architecture in performing multi-modal image segmentation. Furthermore, the method's performance is evaluated on an unseen dataset, showcasing its capacity to generalize and produce accurate segmentations in both modalities. The study highlights the potential of the CDGAN framework in various segmentation applications, particularly those involving multiple imaging modalities. Sequential action prediction poses a difficult forecasting challenge due to the inherent unpredictability of future human actions. Current methods using Markov Decision Processes have limitations, as they assume the ability to make decisions based on a complete state description and a fixed decision-making process. To overcome these constraints, we introduce a new approach, Feature Mapping RNN, which combines a radial basis function kernel to transform the state space and a RNN to model the action sequence. This model can learn the representation of state-action information and predict future actions with the optimized representation. Experimental results show significant improvements over existing methods on benchmarks such as the MiniGrid platform and the Charades dataset. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/zhengyuliu/fmrnn.

This research focuses on developing an effective model for temporal knowledge graph completion by incorporating a model-agnostic and low-rank representation. To achieve this, we introduce the Temporal Entity Embedding Framework (TEEF), which utilizes a low-rank temporal dimension to represent entities and time. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of TEEF over state-of-the-art models across three datasets. Additionally, we provide a deeper analysis of the model's performance using a case study. We propose parity-symmetry-protected package emission, a previously unexplored phenomenon, where multiple qubits simultaneously emit non-trivial, symmetric photons in a condensed state. This phenomenon is observed in a parity-symmetric array of atoms or qubits, interacting with a one-dimensional cavity, where the qubits are initialized in an evenly distributed superposition of states with parity p. When the qubits emit photons, the system maintains parity p, resulting in a bundle of symmetric photons. This phenomenon is confirmed by numerical simulations and has potential applications in quantum communication. Additionally, we investigate the effects of imperfections on the package emission and find that it can still occur under moderate imperfections, with a notable decrease in emission rate. However, significant imperfections will likely prevent the package emission. In the context of distributed systems, network scale estimation is a fundamental problem 
that has been studied under fault-free conditions and random faults. This paper explores 
the problem under the more complex scenario of Byzantine faults, where malicious nodes can 
manipulate and distort information exchanged over the network. We present two accurate 
algorithms for network scale estimation that can withstand Byzantine faults: a direct 
approach and an indirect approach. The direct approach relies on a consensus mechanism, 
yielding a logarithmic complexity and an error rate of O(Δ/ n), where Δ represents the 
network diameter and n is the network size. The indirect approach leverages a distributed 
hash function, achieving a more precise result with an error rate of O(1/n). Notably, both 
algorithms demonstrate robustness against a wide range of malicious nodes, including up to 
n/3 faults in the direct approach and up to (n-1)/2 faults in the indirect approach. We 
demonstrate the efficacy of these algorithms through experiments on a small-world network model. 
The indirect approach is particularly efficient, running in a linear number of rounds and 
enabling accurate scale estimation. The paper also provides a theoretical analysis of the 
indirect approach's precision and the trade-offs involved in designing this algorithm. The 
experiments show that the indirect approach outperforms the direct approach in terms of 
round complexity while achieving comparable error rates. The paper also compares its 
performance to a baseline approach using a hash function without any consensus mechanism, 
demonstrating improved error rates and more stable results. The indirect approach is 
considered the most efficient solution due to its optimal round complexity and better error 
performance. The paper also presents an extension of the indirect approach, enhancing its 
stability against Byzantine faults by introducing a novel mechanism to detect and prevent 
sabotage. The paper showcases the effectiveness of this extension through experiments on a 
small-world network model, highlighting its improved error rates and more reliable results.

prevent malicious behavior. The paper also presents an alternative to the indirect approach,

effectiveness of this alternative through experiments on a small-world network model,

We introduce the Constant Time Kinematics method, an innovative approach to tackle the underdetermined initial data problem in numerical relativity. This method utilizes constraints from the Hamiltonian and momentum equations to solve for arbitrary lapse and shift profiles. We demonstrate that enforcing these constraints results in a fully overdetermined system of equations. Our analysis includes a comprehensive examination of the method's properties and numerical effectiveness. We successfully apply the Constant Time Kinematics method to a range of simple scenarios, including underdetermined spherically symmetric models and spinning black holes. Our findings show that this method can efficiently solve for lapse and shift profiles with minimal dependence on initial conditions. We also observe that using the Constant Time Kinematics method leads to improved convergence rates in numerical relativity simulations. Furthermore, we show that this approach can be adapted to accommodate a variety of metric symmetries. We anticipate that the Constant Time Kinematics method will be a valuable tool for researchers working on numerical relativity problems. Our code implementing this method is freely available at https://github.com/cttk-ctk/cttk.leaf.

Multidimensional time series forecasting is a complex task that often suffers from low data quality, scarce historical data, and a high dimensionality of data in various fields like weather and electricity price analysis. To tackle this complexity, we propose an innovative framework that dynamically constructs an interaction graph from time series data. This graph reflects the non-linear, anisotropic connections between series influenced by noise and random fluctuations. To identify significant correlations, we develop a protocol that adapts the graph structure and includes only robust interactions for multidimensional forecasting. We also introduce a novel optimization technique for the graph's parameters, leveraging the time series' own features to enhance prediction accuracy. Experimental results demonstrate our method's superiority over established models in various scenarios. Furthermore, we showcase the effectiveness of our approach in time series forecasting by achieving a 12% improvement in MAE over the state-of-the-art on the M4 dataset. Additionally, we achieve a 10% improvement in MAE on the hourly electricity price dataset and a 6% improvement in MAE on the weather dataset. We investigate the linear basis pursuit problem in an infinite-dimensional space, specifically in R^n to infinity, where n is finite and greater than 0. The problem seeks the sparsest solution with minimal non-zero components to an underdetermined equation. Traditional research assumes a countable basis, but our study considers a continuum basis. We demonstrate that for any given basis, there either exists a unique sparse solution or an abundance of distinct sparse solutions. Additionally, we present a continuous basis with numerous distinct sparse solutions. Furthermore, we define a property for complete metric spaces, 'CP', which ensures the uniqueness of sparse solutions, and show that countable bases satisfy this 'CP' property. We also provide an example of a countable basis that fails to satisfy 'CP', and surprisingly, an 'CP' property for countable bases that is stronger than the usual requirement of linearly independent vectors. Finally, we propose an 'CP2' property, which guarantees the convergence of a particular iterative algorithm in complete metric spaces with 'CP', and demonstrate that countable bases satisfy 'CP2'. We then compare 'CP' and 'CP2' to other existing properties in complete metric spaces. Along the way, we establish a general method to show the convergence of iterative algorithms in complete metric spaces with a contractive function. This research significantly expands the existing literature on the basis pursuit problem in complete metric spaces with a contractive function. It also provides a new perspective on the sparsity constraint in functional analysis. Ultimately, this study contributes to the broader field of functional analysis. A precise numerical solution for the vector transport equation is achieved using the lowest-order Raviart-Thomas elements, which build upon a novel approach for the vector identity equation. This approach is then adapted for the transport equation, yielding an unconditionally stable scheme with a second-order accuracy on the lowest-order quadrilateral Raviart-Thomas elements. Furthermore, a post-processing technique is developed to enhance the accuracy of the computed vector field without modifying the underlying finite element discretisation. Specifically, if the exact solution is smooth enough, the modified scheme achieves a fourth-order accuracy. Numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the effectiveness of the post-processing technique in improving the solution quality. As a decentralized machine learning approach, federated learning bypasses the need for sensitive data to be stored in the cloud, instead allowing it to remain on local devices. This framework comprises three interconnected components: it necessitates fairness in model development across all participating devices, requires data protection, and involves a substantial number of data owners whose behavior cannot be predicted. The integration of differential privacy and fairness constraints in federated learning presents a complex optimization problem, with solutions often being approximations rather than exact solutions. Recent breakthroughs in fairness-aware federated learning have led to the development of new optimization methods, with some utilizing differential privacy to safeguard against data exposure. However, existing research in this area remains fragmented and there is a lack of comprehensive surveys on this topic. This paper aims to bridge this knowledge gap by providing an in-depth review of the current state of research in fairness-aware federated learning, with a focus on constraint-based and utility-bandit approaches. We also examine the intersection of differential privacy and fairness in FL, highlighting the trade-offs involved and presenting key challenges and future research directions in this area. Furthermore, we outline the key challenges and opportunities for future research in this field. This paper is an expanded version of our initial survey, with additional content and new research insights incorporated. We investigate a variant of the Stable Roommates problem, where agents' preferences are additive and separable. This means each agent's preference is the sum of three separate components. In the optimization-generalization paradox, overfitting models that excel on the training set consistently underperform on unseen data. Our research introduces a family of wealth functions that generate diverse feature distributions based on ranking model predictions. In this research, we investigate how common flaws in photonic devices impact the results of cross-correlation spectroscopy and present methods to mitigate these flaws, allowing for more accurate interpretations of the resulting auto-correlation spectra. A general framework is developed to identify potential issues and their effects, along with specific strategies to address common problems in photonics. These solutions are initially applied to the case of astrophotonic spectroscopy. Additionally, we outline potential areas for further research to improve the accuracy of astrophotonic spectroscopy. This work is expected to contribute to the development of more robust and accurate photonics-based spectroscopic methods. Deep generative models have shown great promise in creating realistic synthetic data, but their application in imitation learning remains limited. Imitation learning aims to teach an agent how to perform a specific task by providing it with examples of the desired behavior. When the environment in which the demonstrations were collected differs from the one the agent needs to perform the task, the problem becomes even more challenging due to differences in observation and action spaces. We present a new method called Cross-Domain Mimicry Network (CDMNet) that can learn to perform a task as shown in observations from pre-recorded demonstrations in a different context. The network learns to bridge the domain gap between what it observes and what it needs to perform by using an adversarial loss, resulting in improved performance compared to previous approaches. The effectiveness of our method is demonstrated through successful imitation of diverse tasks, including reaching, door opening, and button pressing, collected under different camera perspectives. We also show that our method outperforms previous approaches in complex scenarios with moving obstacles. The synthetic trajectories generated by our method serve as a short-cut for agents to learn complex paths that would be difficult to achieve through reinforcement learning. Achieving compatibility in fashion images is crucial for avoiding visually distracting outcomes. Most existing methods treat compatibility as a binary classification task, but this approach is limited as it only considers two categories. We introduce a new task called visual incompatibility identification, which involves identifying all incompatible items. Our proposed model, VICTOR, is a unique transformer architecture that addresses this new task. It consists of two key components: a fashion-aware pre-trained language model and a custom-designed multi-layer transformer. The former captures long-term fashion characteristics through contrastive learning, while the latter enables the identification of incompatible items by leveraging feature interactions. Our experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art models on the Fashion-Incompatibility dataset. Additionally, we showcase the potential applications of our model in the field of computer vision. Our code and pre-trained models are available for download at https://github.com/zhaozhuyu/FashionIncompatibility.

Federated Learning can be implemented using the Buffered Asynchronous Aggregation (BAA) protocol, which enables a server to collect local model updates from clients and aggregate them asynchronously. The original BAA algorithm only allows the server to update its gradient buffer with the current client model's gradient, which must be calculated using the latest client data. This restriction limits the server's ability to process slower client gradients, leading to underutilization of computational resources. Our research builds upon this concept by introducing an unrestricted gradient update rule in the server, allowing it to process gradients from various model versions. This results in a more efficient protocol, which we have tested in a federated learning setting. Our experiments show that the new protocol, Unrestricted BAA (UBA), can outperform BAA in terms of communication efficiency and computational resource utilization. Notably, UBA achieves comparable or better performance in several benchmark datasets, including MNIST, CIFAR-10, and EMNIST. This improvement is attributed to the server's ability to process multiple client gradients concurrently, which accelerates the learning process. Furthermore, UBA demonstrates robustness in the presence of slow clients and heterogeneous device memory. Our source code is publicly available on GitHub. This research was supported in part by an NSERC Canada Research Chair.

To facilitate this inference, knowledge graph embeddings can be used, but this typically necessitates training separate models for GAE and LAE. We propose a unified model that combines both, allowing for the implicit inference of relationships without the need for additional training. This unification is achieved through pre-training a single model to perform inferential tasks, including predicting entities that can be linked to input entities via implicit relationships. The effectiveness of this model is demonstrated in a question-answering task, where it outperforms a baseline model that only predicts explicit relationships. We analyze the dynamics of a stratified shear flow with viscosity, given a randomly perturbed free surface. Viscosity in this context causes vertical momentum distribution to become smoother. A general approach for describing such systems is the Birkhoff-Lewis equation, which governs the evolution of a flow's surface under perturbations. However, solving this equation is computationally complex, so we focus on developing a simplified model based on the Birkhoff-Lewis equation. This model, which we call the 'physical optics approximation,' significantly reduces computational demands while accurately representing certain aspects of the Birkhoff-Lewis dynamics. Our analysis shows that the physical optics approximation accurately describes the physical dynamics in weakly stratified systems with small Rossby numbers. A numerical example demonstrates the physical optics approximation's ability to capture non-trivial dynamics in this regime. Furthermore, we discuss the physical optics approximation's relevance to geophysical flows with low Rossby numbers. To combat the spread of false information, it is crucial to identify tweets that promote unverified vaccine claims and convey the correct information to the original posters. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on the newly created dataset, surpassing the performance of models that focus solely on each task. Notably, our results indicate that identifying unverified vaccine claims and determining acceptance or rejection are interconnected goals. In addition, we provide an analysis of the characteristics of unverified vaccine claims and demonstrate that our approach can effectively generalize to other domains. The code and dataset are available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/nyuclabml/vax-accept-reject.

Physics-informed neural networks have shown remarkable potential in solving partial differential equations. However, physics-informed neural networks face challenges when dealing with equations that involve spatial operators with varying dimensions, as this usually requires a significant number of nodes in the network to accurately capture the dynamics. To address this issue, we present a new adaptive node creation method called Residual-based Adaptive Node creation using Graphs. This approach dynamically adds nodes to the physics-informed neural network based on the residual errors at each point in the domain, resulting in a more compact and efficient network architecture that achieves higher accuracy with fewer nodes. Our experiments demonstrate that this method significantly outperforms existing node creation methods in solving various types of partial differential equations. Furthermore, we provide a theoretical analysis of the method's convergence properties. The code for this method is available on GitHub at https://github.com/rahulr22/RANG.

The Cargo Ecosystem is the largest Java dependency library, comprising over 183,000 projects and 1.4 million Maven artifacts, directly connected to 80% of Java's open-source codebase. To enhance security, we developed a Dependency-Weakness Knowledge Graph (DWKG) to map dependencies to known weaknesses and graph algorithms to identify vulnerability transmission. The DWKG was constructed from Cargo dependency information and 34,000 weaknesses, with our analysis showing that 6.4% of vulnerabilities were transmitted to at least one downstream dependency in the graph. Our findings were validated through case studies of 12 high-risk dependencies, revealing 1,321 previously unreported vulnerability transmissions. Manual audits of top 1% risky dependencies in the Cargo Ecosystem revealed 14% of them had not been updated in over two years, with 83% of their vulnerabilities still unaddressed. Our research contributes to the development of the DWKG and transitivity-based vulnerability propagation framework to aid Cargo Ecosystem maintainers in updating dependencies and preventing vulnerability transmissions. Our source code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/secure-software-cord/cargo-weakness-graph. This research was supported by NSF Grant 2020279. The success of Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) heavily relies on an accurate graph convolution function. In the context of 3D point cloud learning, the conventional Euclidean gradient-based GCN falls short due to its inefficiencies in data representation and high computational requirements. This study introduces an alternative graph convolution function, GCN-I, which employs the inverse multivariate interpolation formula to combine neighboring points on the surface of a 3D shape, thereby improving the GCN framework. The proposed method is then applied to point cloud GCNs and demonstrated to achieve superior performance in basic operations such as mean, sum, and multiplication, outperforming the existing GCN framework by a significant margin. Furthermore, our method exhibits substantial efficiency improvements, specifically a 6 times speedup over the previous approach while maintaining comparable accuracy. The source code for this study has been made publicly available.

Deep neural networks are vulnerable to Trojan attacks that embed backdoors in
trained models without affecting their performance. Most current defense methods
target specific Trojan patterns, assuming that the trigger pattern is fixed and
can be identified. However, this is impractical as attackers can use semantic
triggers that integrate with normal input data, and the embedded backdoors become
difficult to detect when the trigger patterns vary. To address this, we propose
a new type of Trojan attack called Semantic Host-less Trojan Attack (SHTA), 
where the trigger pattern is undefined and model triggers are tied to semantic
attributes. We also introduce a corresponding defense strategy that focuses on
detecting hidden backdoors without relying on specific trigger patterns. Our
experimental results show that SHTA achieves higher success rates and more robust
stability compared to traditional Trojan attacks, while our defense method
significantly outperforms existing methods in detecting hidden backdoors. Our
source code is available at https://github.com/zhaozhhy/SHTA.

We have adapted this approach to the GM policy iteration algorithm and termed it inexact GM policy iteration. Our method ensures that the approximate solution remains nearly optimal, while reducing the computational burden associated with exact algorithms. We have also conducted comprehensive experiments to demonstrate its practical efficacy. inquiries have been proposed, allowing the model to gather information about 
specific training inputs before making predictions. However, the trade-offs between 
information gain, noise resilience, and computational cost are complex. We

advantages in situations where models face significant perturbations but have 
access to label information for individual training samples. We also provide a 
method for determining the optimal balance between information and safety. Our 
experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of local inquiries in such 
robust learning scenarios. The code for our experiments is available online at

We introduce a new method to assess the performance of spectral energy distribution fitting tools for estimating star formation rates in galaxies. To improve future SED-fitting techniques, we suggest incorporating AGN templates and considering additional physical processes affecting the SFR calculation. Ultimately, we believe that the proposed method will serve as a reliable benchmark for evaluating the performance of SED-fitting algorithms. This paper introduces a novel method for generating speech duration synthetic data based on a non-parametric median absolute deviation technique. In recent years, deep learning has become a preferred approach for multimodal
machine learning tasks. Despite numerous studies on multimodal neural networks,
many of them focus on linearly combining different modalities, which can result
in significant information loss. To address this issue, we propose a new
framework called the Generalized K-fan Multimodal Neural Network, which allows
for non-linear combination of modalities through the K-fan layer. This new
network features a shared representation for improved learning of common
features and efficient fusion of non-linear modalities. We also introduce
optimization techniques tailored to the K-fan layer to enhance training. Our
experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed network on two
datasets, achieving superior performance compared to state-of-the-art models.

The rapid dissemination of information on WhatsApp, a popular messaging app, plays a significant role in disseminating rumors in India, which have occasionally triggered violent consequences. In an attempt to curb the spread of misinformation, WhatsApp introduced a feature limiting message forwarding to five chats. This study evaluates the effectiveness of this change by collecting a dataset of highly forwarded messages in India during the 2019 general election period. Our analysis indicates that the new policy primarily slowed down the dissemination of extremely popular messages, particularly those exceeding 700 forwards. However, it had a negligible impact on messages with 700 forwards or less, which continue to be forwarded rapidly. Furthermore, our results suggest that the policy shift led to a temporary decrease in the number of unique chats forwarding these messages, but this effect faded over time. In addition, we found that the policy change did not significantly hinder the spread of existing, highly forwarded messages. However, it did delay the forwarding of new messages by approximately one day. This study's findings provide insight into WhatsApp's policy impact and lay the groundwork for more comprehensive research on the platform's policy interventions. In the process, we also introduce a new method for collecting WhatsApp messages, which can be employed to study various phenomena, as well as policy evaluations in the future. Superconducting quantum circuits are highly regarded for their quantum coherence, 
making them suitable for quantum information processing and serving as sensitive 
environmental detectors. In order to improve and control these circuits, a 
non-invasive method to measure their tiny parameters is essential. We have 
developed a terahertz scanning probe based on near-field scanning microscopy 
capable of measuring sub-micron scale components of superconducting quantum 
circuits with high spatial resolution. This technique was successfully applied 
to analyze the local electrical properties of a 3D microstrip resonator. The 
results showed that this technique can identify microscopic features such as 
thin film losses and micro-fabrication errors. We have also observed the 
electrical field distribution in a 1 GHz resonant circuit with high frequency 
resolution. This technique can be applied to investigate other types of 
terahertz quantum circuits and even classical systems. With further advancements, 
this technique has the potential to measure even smaller scale components.

Federated learning is a decentralized machine learning approach that enables a global server model to update its parameters by aggregating local client model parameters from multiple clients. In this research, we introduce a zero-shot federated learning framework for audio classification tasks. It allows the global server model to access new classes of data stored on client devices, enablin it to incorporate knowledge from these novel classes. A comprehensive performance evaluation of our framework was conducted on four benchmark datasets, comparing it to conventional federated learning and zero-shot learning methods. The results demonstrate that our framework outperforms baseline methods by a significant margin, specifically by 5.7% and 3.1% in terms of accuracy on SLAM dataset and LibriSpeech respectively, with a substantial reduction in communication cost of up to 87%. We introduce xor filters, a new family of approximate membership filters, outperforming both Bloom and Cuckoo filters in speed and size efficiency. Our membership filters utilize hash functions to store and query elements, similar to Bloom filters, but use bitwise xor operations instead of modular arithmetic. This leads to significantly faster lookup times, especially when hash function calculations are involved. Additionally, our xor filters require less space to achieve the same false positive rates, making them more storage-efficient. Our experiments confirm the excellent performance of xor filters, with a 30% reduction in processing time and a 20-50% reduction in memory usage compared to Bloom filters. Interestingly, xor filters can be seen as a variant of Cuckoo filters, with our design offering improved lookup times and reduced memory requirements. A C-xor filter, combining the strengths of Cuckoo and xor filters, also demonstrates superior performance, with faster query times and higher efficiency than Bloom filters. The source code for our xor filters is available on GitHub at https://github.com/chenliu2021/xor_filter. Our evaluation results can be accessed at https://chenliu2021.github.io/xor_filter_eval. This work introduces a method to evaluate the accuracy of generalized polynomial chaos expansions (GPC) outside of the initial approximation stage. Our approach generates a confidence interval for the partial sum of the expansions using classical error estimates and Navier-Stokes solution convergence criteria. This method is demonstrated by verifying a GPC representation of the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations in a finite domain with initial condition error and external data perturbation factors. The associated error analysis relies on the smoothness properties of the solutions to these equations, which are known to be $W^{2,\infty}$. The results of this study confirm the effectiveness of our proposed method in assessing the accuracy of the GPC representations. The corresponding numerical implementation is detailed, along with a comprehensive set of test cases that demonstrate the method's utility. We present a new primal-dual algorithm for solving constrained Markov decision processes in a finite setting with or without partial state information. The approach adapts the primal-dual method from convex optimization by incorporating a constrained policy gradient technique. Each iteration yields a policy with increased primal value or improved constraint compliance. The dual variable also experiences augmentation. The algorithm achieves a polylogarithmic gap closure in a finite time, which can be attributed to the application of the Gloriant polynomial. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through numerical experiments involving a class of approximate dynamic programming schemes. The particular scheme used is one variant of the adaptive value and policy iteration method. The analysis also extends to the case with partial state information by incorporating a structural assumption on the constraint. The method's performance in this context is compared with a recent scheme based on the Frank-Wolfe method. The results show that the new method outperforms the benchmark in both scenarios. Self-supervised pre-training has been proven to be highly effective for deep neural networks.  A key component of this method involves extracting hidden characteristics from data that are informative enough to achieve high performance on downstream tasks.  A recent approach using Vision Transformer (ViT) architecture has shown promising results, however, the underlying characteristics of this model remain poorly understood.  Through extensive analysis of the first ViT-based self-supervised method, which relies on CLS-contrast, we identify several critical factors contributing to its success.  These factors include the ability of the model to derive novel attributes from data, the influence of pre-training data quality, and the role of downstream task similarity to the initial task.  Our study also highlights the challenges inherent to ViT and proposes potential solutions to improve its performance.  Our code and models are publicly available for reproduction of our experimental results.

Diffusion models excel at generating highly realistic images, but their stability issues during training often lead to model failures before completion. We address these stability concerns in diffusion models by introducing a single, reliable objective function that balances sampling and learning processes. This objective function, known as the stable creator, relies on a single image dataset and achieves equilibrium between sampling and learning, resulting in a stable and predictable output transformation across sampling steps. We also demonstrate that the stable creator's latent space has a clear semantic structure, which can be utilized to create diverse dataset variations through straightforward manipulation of the latent code. Our model outperforms existing creators in diffusion models, particularly in text-conditioned scenarios, and shows significant improvements in stability during training, as well as the ability to control sampling step outputs with high semantic coherence. Our model's source code is available at https://github.com/aleksandergryadun/stable-creator.

This model uses a minimal film-based representation and a basic predictive model, outperforming existing state-of-the-art models. Our findings provide insight into the relationship between human vision and dynamic recognition models, and highlight the importance of developing methods that can identify and utilize meaningful representations. In the context of compact binary mergers, specifically white dwarf-black hole mergers, we investigate the spectral characteristics of white dwarfs accreting onto black holes. Our analysis is grounded in the real-world merger event of CVn V, which involved a white dwarf and a black hole. We employ white dwarf models from the MESA framework to simulate various masses and surface temperatures, and then apply the ATOM models to compute synthetic spectra. Our simulations of CVn V's white dwarf reveal a mass of approximately 0.18 solar masses and a surface temperature of about 5,000 Kelvin. We observe that the white dwarf's spectral features are primarily influenced by hydrogen and helium, with metal abundance playing a relatively minor role. The challenge will be part of the ICCV 2023 conference and will offer substantial prizes to drive innovation in this complex analysis domain. To facilitate cross-lingual transfer in NLP, we developed NT-PR, a neural task
representation framework that can be used without modification in any model. NT-PR
defines a task representation as a set of neural networks, one for each source
language, and achieves cross-lingual transfer by minimizing the difference in
task representations between languages. We tested NT-PR on three tasks - sentiment
analysis, question-answering, and named entity recognition - in English, Spanish,
and Portuguese, with and without a teacher model, and found it to be an
effective method of model-agnostic cross-lingual transfer. NT-PR performed better
than existing methods, and even with no teacher model, it successfully applied
the task representation to a student model of a different language. When paired
with a teacher model, NT-PR improved task accuracy by as much as 20% on
unsupervised data. We also found that NT-PR can be used to improve task
accuracy in cases of limited labeled data, and that it can even be used to
cross-lingually transfer ensemble models. We have made NT-PR available under the

To tackle the challenge of video super-resolution, we have developed a method that leverages information from all frames to restore high-resolution images from low-quality video inputs. Building on the success of BasicVSR, our approach employs a compact 3D spatial propagation structure and decoders with residual learning to improve accuracy. Additionally, we have introduced frame reordering and feature alignment techniques to enhance the quality of the output and adapt the model to x4 downsampling factor. In our experiments, we have achieved state-of-the-art performance on various metrics, including PSNR and SSIM, while reducing computational complexity and model size compared to previous methods. Our source code is available on GitHub for public use.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using a single global model can cause performance degradation when switching between tasks due to interference from previous experiences. Our research introduces a novel approach where each task has its own local model, connected in a modular network, which prevents interference and enables efficient knowledge transfer. We provide theoretical justification for this design through the lens of catastrophic interference and show its efficacy in a range of complex multi-task reinforcement learning experiments. This method can be applied to deep RL environments by treating it as a regularization technique. Our code is publicly available.

To address these complexities, we present a novel approach called USBR, which utilizes bicluster analysis to discover and personalize user preferences while accounting for their contextual structure. Our method effectively handles the inherent sparsity and subjectivity of user preference data by incorporating a user-specific and item-specific loss function. Experimental evaluations demonstrate the superiority of USBR over state-of-the-art techniques in both predictive accuracy and diversity. Additionally, our method is scalable and adaptable to various types of preference data and bicluster algorithms. This paper introduces a novel neural network approach that learns to map images from one style to another by utilizing two operations: forward style transfer and reverse hue mapping. The forward transfer converts a source image's style, captured through a global color image, into a target style. The reverse hue mapping utilizes a target style mask to revert a image back to its original style or a different style. The network is trained using paired images, but utilizes self-similarities within individual images to improve its performance. The method is applied to two tasks: converting image colors and reversing camouflage patterns. The results show that the method surpasses state-of-the-art style transfer techniques in color transfer and achieves comparable results to current camouflage reversal methods while being faster and more efficient. The method is also shown to be effective in reverse hue mapping tasks. The code for this method is available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/zhengyuliu/StyleDistillation.

In autonomous robot navigation, actively selecting observations can significantly reduce the number of sensory inputs needed, making data processing more efficient. We present a novel framework that integrates a prediction model and an observation selection model, allowing robots to choose relevant sensory data and anticipate future states. This results in more compact sensory datasets and improved prediction capabilities. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through successful application to a simple simulated robot, achieving observation selection rates of up to 80% and accurate predictions of 90% using only 10 out of 100 possible observations. This framework offers a general solution for active sensing in autonomous systems. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/alexkamaldeep/ActivePrediction.

Additionally, we explore the relationship between our approach and existing continuous-time Q-learning methods. Accurate vertebrae localization and identification in CT scans are crucial for various clinical applications like radiation therapy planning, fracture assessment, and spinal degeneration analysis. However, this task is often challenging due to the varying poses of patients and the similar appearances of vertebrae. To address this issue, we have developed a fully automated CT-based system for identifying and categorizing vertebrae. The process begins by transforming the pelvic region into a standardized orientation to ensure consistent spinal alignment. Next, a mathematical optimization technique is employed to determine the positions of the vertebrae based on anatomical constraints and a spine model. The results are then fine-tuned using 3D morphological analysis. The effectiveness of our approach was evaluated using a large dataset of 1,000 CT scans, which contained 1,600 labeled vertebrae. The results showed that our system surpassed the performance of a leading deep learning-based method and accurately localized and identified 96.5% of all vertebrae with an average error of 4.5 mm. We introduce Amanuensis, a novel approach to automate code education by incorporating human-like corrections. Current code review tools primarily focus on detecting and resolving issues, whereas code education involves guiding novice programmers through their mistakes. Amanuensis, an advanced trainee, is designed to learn from a human instructor via interactive human-in-the-loop corrections. By applying reinforcement learning, Amanuensis refines its correction policy to better align with its human instructor's feedback. Our case studies demonstrate that Amanuensis can effectively learn to provide insightful, actionable suggestions for code debugging and educational purposes. Additionally, we have made our implementation available to the public. Further research is needed to explore the potential of Amanuensis as a code tutor. Amanuensis is currently an online service that accepts C and Java submissions. It is accessible through our website at https://amanuensis.cs.cmu.edu/. A detailed description of our approach is provided in our paper, which has been published in the proceedings of ICSE 2022.
